title: Your first DataFrame

concept_blocks.html: Welcome aboard. Everything you run here is real pandas, executing right in your browser — no server, no setup. Three tables are already loaded and waiting for you: customers, deals, and reps. Each one is a DataFrame: a rectangular grid of data with named columns and numbered rows, a lot like a spreadsheet you can talk to in code.
The friendliest way to meet a DataFrame is .head(), which shows the first few rows so you can eyeball the shape of things without printing hundreds of lines. Try it on customers:

Three attributes tell you the lay of the land. .shape gives a (rows, columns) tuple, .columns lists the column names, and .dtypes reports each column’s type — notice that signup_date is a real datetime64, not just text. Getting fluent with these three is how you orient yourself in any unfamiliar table.

title: Selecting columns

concept_blocks.html: A whole DataFrame is a fine thing to look at, but usually you only care about a column or two. Reach for a single column by name with square brackets — customers["city"] — and pandas hands you back a Series: a one-dimensional labeled column, index on the left and values on the right.

Now watch what happens when you pass a list of names inside the brackets. customers[["city"]] — note the double brackets — gives you a DataFrame instead, a table that just happens to have one column. That is the key distinction: df["col"] (a string) returns a Series, while df[["col"]] (a list) returns a DataFrame. The list form scales to as many columns as you name.

One more thing worth internalizing: the order you list the columns is the order you get them back. Asking for ["city", "name"] puts city first, even though name comes earlier in the original frame. You choose the shape of the output — which columns, and in what order.

title: Label vs position: .loc and .iloc

concept_blocks.html: Square brackets on a frame pick columns. To reach for rows — or rows and columns together — pandas gives you two accessors, and the difference between them is worth burning into memory. .iloc works by integer position, exactly like slicing a Python list: customers.iloc[:5] means “the first five rows,” whatever their labels happen to be. .loc works by label — the actual index values and column names — and it also understands boolean masks.

concept_blocks.code:
# .iloc is positional: the first 5 rows, all columns
customers.iloc[:5]

concept_blocks.html: .loc is the label-aware sibling. Its real power shows up with two arguments — df.loc[rows, cols] — letting you carve out specific rows and specific columns in one move. The row selector can be a boolean mask (a condition), and the column selector a list of names. Here we take Won deals over $30k and keep just three columns:

For a single cell, either accessor takes a row-then-column pair: customers.iloc[0, 1] pulls the value at the first row, second column by position, while customers.loc[0, "name"] asks for it by label. The rule of thumb: reach for .iloc when you’re thinking in positions and offsets, and .loc when you’re thinking in names and conditions.

title: Filtering with boolean masks

concept_blocks.html: Selecting columns narrows a table sideways. Filtering rows narrows it downward — keep only the records that pass some test. In pandas you do this in two steps that are worth seeing separately. First, a comparison on a column produces a boolean mask: a Series of True/False, one value per row.
That mask lines up with the frame row-for-row. Hand it back to the frame with df[mask] and pandas keeps only the rows where the mask is True — every column comes along for the ride:

Any comparison operator builds a mask: == (equal), != (not equal), >, <, >=, <=. Note the doubled == for equality — a single = is assignment. You will often write the comparison straight inside the brackets, as in deals[deals["amount"] > 20000], once the two-step idea is familiar.

task_html: Return every column of deals where amount is greater than 30000 — the biggest opportunities on the board.
hint: Build a boolean mask with deals["amount"] > 30000, then index the frame with it: deals[mask].

All three alt_solutions graded PASS/match against the reference: the two-step mask variable form, the `.loc[...]` form, and `deals.query(\"amount > 30000\")`. title: Sorting with sort_values

concept_blocks.html: Rows come out of a DataFrame in whatever order they were stored. When you want them ranked — newest first, biggest at the top, alphabetical — reach for sort_values. You hand it the column to sort by, and it returns a new DataFrame with the rows rearranged; the original is left untouched.
That sorts ascending by default — smallest to largest, and for dates that means oldest first. Flip it with ascending=False to put the largest (or most recent) value at the top:

Sort by several columns at once by passing a list. Pandas breaks ties left to right — it orders by the first column, and only when two rows tie does the second column decide. You can even give each its own direction with a matching list of booleans:

title: Top-N with nlargest

concept_blocks.html: Often you don’t want the whole table sorted — you just want the few biggest (or smallest) rows. nlargest does exactly that in one step: it finds the top n rows by a column and hands them back already ordered largest-first.

The classic long-hand is to sort the whole frame and then take the head: sort_values("amount", ascending=False) puts the biggest on top, and .head(3) keeps the first three. Same rows, same order — nlargest is just the tidy shortcut.

Both give you the full rows. To keep only the columns you care about, tack on a column selection: deals.nlargest(3, "amount")[["deal_id", "amount"]]. When order is the whole point, finish with .reset_index(drop=True) so the row numbers read 0, 1, 2 instead of the original scattered index.

title: Combining conditions

concept_blocks.html: One boolean mask filters on a single test. Real questions usually stack several: “Won and big”, “this country or that one”. You combine masks with & (and) and | (or) — but pandas has one firm rule here: wrap each condition in its own parentheses. Without them, Python’s operator precedence runs & before the comparisons and you get a confusing error instead of a filter.

When you’re testing one column against a list of allowed values, chaining | gets clumsy fast. .isin([...]) is the clean way to say “is this value one of these?” — it returns a boolean mask just like a comparison does. And for a numeric range, .between(lo, hi) reads better than two comparisons joined with & (both ends are inclusive).

title: String methods (.str)

concept_blocks.html: A column of text is a Series of strings, and pandas gives every such Series a .str accessor — a doorway to string operations that run on every row at once. Reach for it whenever you want to ask a text question of a whole column: .str.contains("Retail") asks “does this value contain Retail?”, and .str.startswith("D") asks “does it begin with D?”. Each one returns a boolean Series, one True/False per row, which is exactly the shape a filter mask needs.

These checks are case-sensitive by default, so .str.contains("retail") would miss "Cascade Retail Group". When you want to ignore capitalization, pass case=False. The example below finds every city containing the letters on in any case — note how it catches both “London” and “Boston”.

title: Missing data (NaT)

concept_blocks.html: When a deal is still open, it has no close date yet — and pandas records that hole with a special marker, NaT (“Not a Time”, the datetime cousin of NaN). It is emphatically not zero, not an empty string, and not the year 1970. It means “there is no value here.” Every open deal in deals carries a NaT in closed_date.

The trap: you cannot find missing values by comparing to them. Any comparison against a missing value returns False, because “unknown == unknown” is itself unknown. So closed_date == pd.NaT never matches a single row — watch it count to zero:

The right tool is .isna(), which returns a boolean Series that is True exactly where the value is missing. Its mirror image is .notna(), True where a value is present. Use them as masks to keep or drop rows:

concept_blocks.code: deals["closed_date"].isna().sum()   # how many deals are still open

concept_blocks.html: And when you want to replace the holes rather than filter them, .fillna(value) swaps every missing entry for a value of your choosing — handy for display, though here we just want to find the open deals.

title: Unique values & value_counts

concept_blocks.html: Real data is full of repetition — the same stage shows up on dozens of deals, the same industry across many customers. Pandas gives you a small family of methods for asking “what are the distinct things here, and how often does each appear?”

Call .unique() on a Series to get a plain array of its distinct values, in the order they first appear — no sorting, no counting. Its companion .nunique() just tells you how many distinct values there are. Reach for .unique() when you want the actual list of categories, and .nunique() when you only care about the count.

When you want the distinct values with their frequencies, use .value_counts(). It returns a Series indexed by each distinct value, sorted from most common to least — a one-line answer to “what’s the breakdown?”

And when the duplicates span whole rows rather than a single column, drop_duplicates() keeps just the first occurrence of each unique row (optionally over a subset of columns). Note the shape difference: .unique() hands you a bare array, while drop_duplicates() preserves the Series or DataFrame it was called on.

title: Aggregating a column

concept_blocks.html: A single column is a Series, and a Series knows how to collapse itself into one number. Reach for .sum(), .mean(), .min(), .max(), or .count() and pandas walks the whole column for you — no loop, just one value back.

concept_blocks.code:
deals["amount"].sum()    # 636000 across all 30 deals
deals["amount"].mean()   # the average deal size
deals["amount"].max()    # the single biggest amount

concept_blocks.html: These methods quietly skip missing values — NaN and NaT are ignored, not treated as zero. That is why .count() is worth knowing: it reports how many non-missing values a column holds. The closed_date column has a NaT for every still-open deal, so counting it tells you how many deals have actually closed.

concept_blocks.code:
deals["deal_id"].count()     # 30 — every deal has an id
deals["closed_date"].count()  # 18 — the 12 open deals (NaT) don't count

concept_blocks.html: To report several numbers at once with their own labels, hand a dictionary to pd.Series. Each key becomes a label, each value the aggregate — one tidy, named result:

title: Grouping with groupby

concept_blocks.html: So far you’ve summarized a whole column at once — one .sum() or .mean() over every row. But often the real question is per category: how many deals in each stage? what’s the average amount per rep? That’s the split–apply–combine pattern, and groupby is how pandas does it. You name a column to split the rows into groups, apply a summary to each group, and pandas combines the answers into one result — one row per group.

The simplest summary is just counting the rows in each group. df.groupby("col").size() returns a Series: the group key becomes the index, and the value is the row count for that group. Notice the index is labeled stage — the grouping column moved out of the data and into the index.

To summarize a specific column instead of just counting, pick the column after grouping: deals.groupby("stage")["amount"].mean() gives the average amount per stage. And when you want several summaries at once, .agg(...) lets you name each output column and pair it with a (column, function) tuple — the result is a tidy DataFrame, still keyed by the group.

title: Filtering groups

concept_blocks.html: You already know how to collapse rows into one number per group with groupby. The next question is a natural one: keep only the groups that pass some test — industries with more than two customers, reps who closed at least five deals, cities with a single account. The idea is aggregate first, then filter the aggregated result.

The cleanest path is two steps you’ve already met. First build a per-group count with groupby(…).size(), which gives a Series indexed by the group key. Then apply a boolean mask to that Series, exactly the way you’d filter any Series.

That leaves you a Series of just the surviving groups. To hand back a tidy two-column table — the group key and its count — call reset_index(name="count"), which turns the index into a column and names the counts.

There’s also a one-shot form, groupby(…).filter(lambda g: len(g) > 2), but note what it returns: the original rows of the passing groups, not the counts. Reach for it when you want the members back; reach for the count-then-mask pattern when you want the summary.

title: Adding & transforming columns

concept_blocks.html: So far you have read from your frames. Now you’ll add to them. The cleanest way to attach a computed column is assign — it returns a new DataFrame with the extra column, leaving the original untouched. The new column is built vectorized: an expression over a whole Series computes every row at once, no loop in sight.

concept_blocks.code:
# amount is in dollars; add a thousands-scaled column next to it
deals.assign(amount_k=deals["amount"] / 1000)[["deal_id", "amount", "amount_k"]].head()

concept_blocks.html: The right-hand side can be any vectorized expression. A comparison like deals["stage"] == "Won" yields a boolean Series — a ready-made flag column. For a two-way choice use np.where(condition, if_true, if_false), and reach for the .dt accessor to pull pieces out of a datetime column, such as .dt.year.

concept_blocks.code:
import numpy as np
deals.assign(
    size=np.where(deals["amount"] >= 30000, "big", "small"),
    open_year=deals["opened_date"].dt.year,
)[["deal_id", "amount", "size", "open_year"]].head()

title: Working with dates (.dt)

concept_blocks.html: Some of your columns aren’t numbers or text at all — they’re real dates. signup_date, opened_date, and closed_date are all stored as datetime64, which means pandas understands them as moments in time, not just strings that happen to look like dates. To reach inside a datetime column and pull out a piece — the year, the month, the day — use the .dt accessor. customers["signup_date"].dt.year hands you back a Series of integer years, one per row, computed all at once.
.dt.month and .dt.day work the same way, so you can crack a date open into its parts and use each part however you like — here, alongside the original column.

Because these are true dates, you can also compare them. Build a moment with pd.Timestamp("2024-01-01") and use it in a boolean mask just like any number — <, >, >= all order dates chronologically, and .between(lo, hi) checks a range. That lets you filter a frame down to rows on one side of a cutoff.

title: Combining DataFrames with merge

concept_blocks.html: So far every question has lived inside a single table. But the interesting facts are spread across frames — a deal knows its rep_id, but the rep’s name lives over in reps. merge stitches two frames together by matching values in a shared column, giving you one wide frame with columns from both sides.

The workhorse call is left.merge(right, on="key"). Here deals and reps both carry a rep_id, so pandas lines up each deal with the rep whose rep_id matches, and glues that rep’s columns onto the deal’s row. By default this is an inner join — only rows that find a match on both sides survive.

The result carries every column from both frames, so you usually finish by selecting just the columns you care about with merged[["amount", "name"]]. One gotcha: if both frames have a column of the same name (other than the key), pandas keeps both and disambiguates them with suffixes — _x and _y by default, or whatever you pass to suffixes=. Chaining a second merge onto customers shows it: both reps and customers have a name, so they land as name_rep and name_customer.

title: Left merge & non-matches

concept_blocks.html: A plain merge keeps only rows that match on both sides — a customer with zero deals simply vanishes from the result. Often that disappearance is exactly the thing you want to find. A left merge (how="left") keeps every row from the left frame no matter what, and fills the right side’s columns with NaN wherever there was no match. So customers.merge(deals, on="customer_id", how="left") keeps all 15 customers; the ones without deals get NaN for deal_id, amount, and the rest.

To see where matches came from, add indicator=True. pandas appends a _merge column labelled "both", "left_only", or "right_only" for each row. The rows you care about are the "left_only" ones — left-side records that found nothing to join to.

concept_blocks.code:
m = customers.merge(deals, on="customer_id", how="left", indicator=True)
m["_merge"].value_counts()

concept_blocks.html: Filtering a left merge down to _merge == "left_only" is the anti-join — “rows on the left with no partner on the right.” It answers questions like “which customers have never had a deal?” A lighter-weight way to write the same idea is a boolean mask with isin: customers[~customers["customer_id"].isin(deals["customer_id"])] keeps customers whose id never appears among the deals. Both give the same answer; the indicator merge is handier when you also want the joined columns alongside.

task_html: Some customers have never generated a single deal. Using a left merge with indicator=True (or an isin anti-join), return just the name of every customer who has no deals at all. Return a DataFrame with the single name column.
hint: Left-merge customers onto deals with indicator=True, keep the rows where _merge equals "left_only", then select [["name"]].
solution:
merged = customers.merge(deals, on="customer_id", how="left", indicator=True)
no_deals = merged[merged["_merge"] == "left_only"]
no_deals[["name"]]

title: Reshaping with pivot_table

concept_blocks.html: Everything so far has produced a long answer — one row per group, one number per row. But questions like “how much money sits in each stage, broken out by industry?” are really a grid: industries down the side, stages across the top, a total in every cell. pivot_table builds that grid in one call. You hand it four things: index (what labels the rows), columns (what labels the columns), values (the numbers to fill the cells), and aggfunc (how to combine when several rows land in the same cell).

Our stage-and-amount data lives in deals, but the industry lives in customers — so we merge first to get an industry column alongside each deal, then pivot. Here we average the amount in each industry×stage cell:

concept_blocks.code:
dealsind = deals.merge(customers[["customer_id", "industry"]], on="customer_id")
dealsind.pivot_table(index="industry", columns="stage", values="amount", aggfunc="mean")

concept_blocks.html: Notice the holes: an industry×stage cell with no deals comes back as NaN. That is rarely what you want in a summary table — a missing combination usually means zero. Pass fill_value=0 to plug those gaps. And margins=True adds a row and column of grand totals (named "All" by default, or whatever you pass as margins_name):

concept_blocks.code:
dealsind = deals.merge(customers[["customer_id", "industry"]], on="customer_id")
dealsind.pivot_table(
    index="industry",
    columns="stage",
    values="amount",
    aggfunc="sum",
    fill_value=0,
    margins=True,
    margins_name="Total",
)

title: Ranking & window ops

concept_blocks.html: Sometimes you want a group-wise calculation but you don’t want to collapse the rows. Every deal should stay a deal — you just want to add a number that answers “where does this row rank within its group?” That’s a window operation, and pandas gives you two workhorses: groupby(...).rank() for positions, and groupby(...).transform(...) for broadcasting a group aggregate back onto every row.

rank() turns values into 1, 2, 3… positions. By default it ranks smallest→first; pass ascending=False to make the largest value rank 1. When you call it after groupby, the numbering restarts inside each group. The method= argument decides how ties are handled — "dense" gives tied values the same rank with no gaps, "min" shares the lowest rank, and "first" breaks ties by row order. Here the deal amounts happen to be distinct within every stage, so all of these agree.

concept_blocks.code:
# a per-group rank column, added without collapsing rows
deals.assign(
    rank_in_stage=deals.groupby("stage")["amount"].rank(method="dense", ascending=False).astype(int)
)[["deal_id", "stage", "amount", "rank_in_stage"]].head()

concept_blocks.html: The companion tool is transform. Where a plain groupby(...).sum() returns one row per group, transform("sum") computes that same per-group total but hands it back aligned to every original row — perfect for “this deal’s amount vs. its stage’s total.” The result always matches the frame’s length, so you can drop it straight into a new column.

concept_blocks.code:
# transform broadcasts a group aggregate back to every row
deals.assign(
    stage_total=deals.groupby("stage")["amount"].transform("sum")
)[["deal_id", "stage", "amount", "stage_total"]].head()

title: Putting it all together

concept_blocks.html: You’ve met every move on its own — filtering with a boolean mask, merge to pull in another table, groupby to split-apply-combine, an aggregate like sum, sort_values, and head for a top-N. A real question rarely needs just one of them. The pandas way is to chain them: each method returns a new DataFrame or Series, so you can hang the next step right off it and read the whole pipeline top to bottom like a recipe.

Say you want the total amount won in each region. Keep only the Won deals, bring in the reps table so every row knows its region, group by that region, and sum the amounts — one flowing expression, no throwaway variables:

Order matters at the finish. When the ask is a leaderboard — biggest first, only the top few — end the chain with sort_values(ascending=False) and head(n). Wrapping the pipeline in parentheses lets you put each step on its own line so a long chain stays readable:

One habit that keeps grading happy: after a groupby the group key becomes the index, so call reset_index to turn it back into a plain column — and use reset_index(name="...") on a Series to name the aggregated column in the same breath.
